posts.title: Financial crime is evolving faster than ever.
posts.author: Shubham Shekhar
posts.snippet:
Financial crime is evolving faster than ever.

From traditional money laundering and fraud to synthetic identities, real time payment fraud, crypto misuse, social engineering, and AI enabled scams, the risk landscape is becoming increasingly complex.

Technology is giving us powerful tools such as AI, machine learning, advanced analytics, automation, biometrics, and real time monitoring.

But technology alone cannot solve financial crime.

The strongest defence comes from the right combination of People + Process + Technology.

As Financial Crime, AML, KYC, Fraud, Risk and Compliance professionals, our role is not just to identify suspicious activity. It is to continuously learn, challenge existing processes, understand emerging risks, and build smarter and more effective controls.

The future of financial crime prevention will belong to organisations that can balance technology with human judgement, data with experience, and innovation with strong governance.

Let’s continue learning, sharing knowledge, and building a safer and more trusted financial ecosystem. 🌍

What do you think will be the biggest financial crime challenge over the next five years?

#FinancialCrime #AML #KYC #FraudPrevention #TransactionMonitoring #RiskManagement #Compliance #FinancialCrimeCompliance #FraudRisk #RegTech #FinTech #AMLProfessionals #KYCProfessionals #RiskProfessionals #ComplianceProfessionals

comments.text: On the crypto side specifically, the People + Process + Technology point holds especially well at the choke-point stage: monitoring flags the wallet, but converting that flag into something a court or exchange will act on still depends on an analyst who understands both the chain and the legal standard of proof.

We see this constantly in tracing work - the tooling correctly flags suspicious flows almost instantly, but the bottleneck is turning that output into a report a prosecutor or exchange compliance team can actually use.

posts.title: They had the power to regulate #Crypto.
posts.author: prabu lingam
posts.snippet:
They had the power to regulate #Crypto.
 Instead, they launched their own coin and
 cashed out on you.

We keep asking "when will crypto get proper regulation?"

Meanwhile,

 the people writing those regulations have been quietly doing this:

Launch a memecoin under their name or party brand

 Let insiders and early wallets load up before public listing
 Hype it on official channels, rallies, social media
 Retail piles in — because if a politician backs it, it must be legit, right?
Price pumps, insiders exit, chart collapses
 Radio silence.
 No refunds.
 No accountability. 
Next election cycle, same playbook.

This isn't a "crypto is a scam" post. 
Crypto isn't the problem. 

Concentrated, unchecked power sitting on top of an unregulated asset class is the problem.

When a private founder rugs a coin, 
it's fraud, full stop, and people call it out immediately.

When a sitting official does the exact same thing, it somehow gets rebranded as "market volatility" or "just a fun community project."

If you have the authority to write the rules, launching a token that trades on your own legitimacy is not innovation. 

It's a conflict of interest with a chart attached.

What do you think — should holding public office bar someone from launching a token entirely? 

Or is disclosure enough?
posts.reason: Thoughtful critique of regulatory capture and crypto fraud by officials attracts legal and compliance audiences interested in enforcement and governance, though not directly about forensics.

comments.text: The mechanism you're describing is textbook insider allocation followed by a liquidity-driven exit, and it's traceable on-chain if anyone bothers to look - wallet clustering and timing analysis around the listing usually shows the pattern clearly, official or not.
Genuine question: would disclosure rules actually change behaviour here, or does the enforcement gap mean disclosed conflicts of interest just become the new cover story?

In tracing work we've looked at similar cases where early wallets funded from the same source load up before a public push - the pattern itself isn't hard to identify, the hard part is getting anyone with authority to act on it when the person involved wrote the rules.

posts.title: Give me a graphic for this. **CRYPTO REGULATION’S BLIND SPOT — PART 4 OF 7**
posts.author: Andrew Walker
posts.snippet:
Give me a graphic for this. **CRYPTO REGULATION’S BLIND SPOT — PART 4 OF 7**

**“Only 1% of Crypto Is Illicit” Does Not Mean 99% Has Been Proven Legitimate**

We often hear that approximately 1% of crypto transaction value is identified or estimated as illicit.

But analytics databases are continuously updated.

Previously unknown wallets become linked to scams.

New laundering networks are discovered.

Historical estimates are revised upward.

The blockchain transactions have not changed.

**Our knowledge of who was behind them has changed.**

So if approximately 1% has been classified as illicit, that does not prove the other 99% is legitimate.

An unidentified wallet is not necessarily legitimate.

**It is simply unidentified.**

The critical question is:

What percentage of criminal activity does the monitoring system fail to identify?

Without knowing that false-negative rate, the true percentage remains uncertain.

\#Crypto #BlockchainAnalytics #Statistics #MoneyLaundering #FinancialCrime
posts.reason: Rigorous analysis of blockchain analytics limitations appeals to compliance, legal and law enforcement audiences evaluating investigation quality and evidentiary standards.

comments.text: This is exactly the distinction we push clients to make in practice - an unidentified wallet is not the same as a clean one, and attribution databases get retroactively updated often enough that yesterday's 'legitimate' flow can become tomorrow's flagged one.

Has anyone tried to model the false-negative rate empirically, say by comparing early attribution snapshots of known scam cases against what analytics providers flagged at the time versus years later?

In casework we regularly trace funds through wallets that were unflagged at the time of the transaction but get linked to a scam cluster months later once new evidence surfaces - the 1% figure was never a ceiling, just a snapshot.

posts.author: Jon Glass
posts.snippet:
A few weeks ago I posted about DOJ's new National Fraud Enforcement Division and the growing federal focus on large-scale fraud. Late last week another development caught my eye: the U.S. and U.K. announced a joint effort to take down international scam centers running investment and crypto fraud, operations DOJ estimates cost Americans roughly $10 billion a year.

(DOJ's press release, "U.S. and UK Launch First-of-Its-Kind Joint Alliance to Dismantle Global Scam Centers," is linked in the comments.)

I think the two are related. The National Fraud Enforcement Division gives DOJ a more coordinated way to go after major fraud domestically, and this U.S.-U.K. effort does something similar internationally, going after the networks behind the fraud instead of individual schemes.

Those networks matter to banks. The fraud may happen somewhere else, but the money still moves through bank accounts, payment platforms, money mules, shell companies, and crypto to get anywhere. Fraud and AML overlap right there, even though most banks still run them as separate programs.

There's a regulatory reason to care too. FinCEN's AML/CFT national priorities already list fraud, cyber-enabled crime, and the laundering networks that support them. Banks should be looking at whether what their fraud teams are seeing actually makes it into BSA risk assessments, monitoring, and investigations.

Banks have talked about bringing fraud and AML closer together for years. This is one more reason to stop treating it as a someday project.

#FinancialCrime #Fraud #AML #BSA #Banking
posts.reason: US-UK anti-scam coalition and fraud-AML convergence directly engages banks, law enforcement and regulators on cross-border investigation networks where Bloctopus' expertise is directly applicable.

comments.text: The overlap you describe shows up clearly in cross-border crypto cases - stablecoin transfers that fraud teams see as isolated incidents often turn out, on chain analysis, to be tied to the same laundering infrastructure that AML teams are separately monitoring under a different risk category.

Do you think the joint DOJ-UK effort will actually change exchange cooperation timelines, or does the bottleneck remain domestic legal process regardless of how coordinated the investigative side becomes?

We've traced proceeds from scam center operations where the money moved through mule accounts, then crypto, then back into fiat within days - by the time a bank's fraud team and AML team compared notes, the funds were already three jurisdictions away.

posts.reason: FinCEN crypto scam data and money-laundering ecosystem analysis directly targets VASPs and compliance officers with actionable forensics and detection frameworks.

comments.text: The BSA report volume alone tells a story: 33,904 filings over roughly two years means front-line compliance teams are already flagging this activity, but the choke point is what happens after the SAR is filed. In tracing work we consistently see the same pattern FinCEN describes - initial deposit at a compliant exchange, rapid conversion, then layering through underground banking networks before it ever touches a foreign VASP. By the time a SAR triggers a freeze request, that layering is often already three or four hops deep.

Tacos in hand, and the market's got a lot going on this week.
 
Bitcoin is holding near $80,000, up roughly 30% from its 2026 lows, and sitting above several major moving averages after weeks of recovery.
 
↳ So what's driving it
 
Institutional demand hasn't slowed down. Spot Bitcoin ETFs pulled in close to $987 million in weekly net inflows, real, sustained buying even as rate concerns build in the background.
 
But the macro picture is getting louder. A stronger than expected August jobs report pushed Fed rate hike odds up sharply, one snapshot put the probability of a September hike at 58%, up from under 50% just a day earlier. That pressure briefly pushed BTC below $80,000 toward $78,600.
 
Around $278 million in leveraged positions got liquidated in a four hour stretch after that report dropped, most of it long positions, which tells you the pullback was amplified by traders caught leaning bullish, not just spot selling.
 
↳ Now for the investment trail
 
Bitcoin's market cap is sitting around $1.58 to $1.6 trillion, with BTC holding close to 57% dominance. That matters because it shows this rally has been led by Bitcoin specifically, not spread evenly across altcoins, a sign of institutional capital favoring the asset it trusts most right now.
 
↳ The indicator to watch
 
All eyes are on the September 11 CPI report, five days before the Fed's policy meeting. A softer inflation number could revive hopes for stable rates and give this rally more room to run. A hot one could do the opposite fast.
 
↳ My thoughts
 
This move has been driven far more by macro data than by anything happening inside crypto itself. Jobs numbers, Treasury yields, rate expectations, they're doing more to shape price right now than any crypto specific headline. Worth watching the CPI print closely, that single data point could decide which way this breaks.

posts.title: CRYPTO LOST $3.63 BILLION.
posts.author: zacky vicent
posts.snippet:
CRYPTO LOST $3.63 BILLION.
THE AUDITS DIDN’T SAVE THEM.

Let that sink in.

Between January 2025 and July 2026, cryptocurrency platforms lost more than $3.63 BILLION to cyberattacks and compromised credentials, according to CoinGecko.

And here’s the fucking absurd part:

A huge portion of the victims had already undergone security audits.

CoinGecko’s August 27 report found that approximately 88% of the stolen funds and around 60% of the affected platforms had completed independent security audits.

So what the hell happened?

The hackers didn’t simply break through the front door.

They attacked the fucking gaps.

Traditional audits often examine systems at a specific point in time. But attackers don’t care about checklists, certificates, or glossy security reports.

They hunt for everything those checks can miss:

Human error.
Compromised credentials.
Operational failures.
Social engineering.
Third-party vulnerabilities.
Access-control weaknesses.
Infrastructure outside the audit’s scope.

And when they find one crack?

BILLIONS FUCKING DISAPPEAR.

THE BIGGEST BLOWS

Bybit — $1.4 BILLION

The largest incident identified in the report.

The February 2025 Bybit theft was linked by blockchain intelligence firm Elliptic to North Korea.

One attack.

$1.4 billion gone.

Then came:

KelpDAO — $292 MILLION

Drift Protocol — $285 MILLION

Three incidents alone account for roughly $1.98 BILLION.

That isn’t some rounding error.

That is nearly $2 BILLION vaporized from the crypto ecosystem.

And the most brutal lesson is this:

A SECURITY AUDIT IS NOT A FORCE FIELD.

A certificate does not stop a hacker.

A compliance report does not protect a private key.

A completed audit does not guarantee that tomorrow’s attack vector will look anything like yesterday’s.

Crypto keeps selling the dream of financial sovereignty while sometimes protecting billions of dollars with security models that were never designed for an environment where attackers operate 24/7/365.

posts.title: You discover the transfer was a scam. Then you make the most dangerous search of the day: “Who can recover my money?”
posts.author: Stella Igwenazor, CISSP, CISA
posts.snippet:
You discover the transfer was a scam. Then you make the most dangerous search of the day: “Who can recover my money?”

That search is not neutral ground. It is a market and it has been waiting for you.

In 2025, Canadians reported losing $25.9 million to recovery-pitch schemes, up from $9.1 million in 2024. The number of reports also rose from 545 to 933.

This is not an isolated problem. It is a growing business built around targeting people who have already been defrauded once. And the re-targeting is often deliberate.

The Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO) has warned that criminal groups maintain lists of previous victims and sell them on. So, when the call comes, the person on the line knows your name, your address and the exact amount you lost. That knowledge feels like proof they are legitimate. It is the opposite.

It is inventory.

The impersonation can be remarkably convincing. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre has warned that fraudsters use its name, logo and letterhead to contact previous victims and offer to recover their money.

The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center has also documented fabricated law firms with professional websites, lawyer profiles and identities borrowed from real lawyers.

A convincing website is not verification. Sometimes, it is the product.

Common warning signs include:
-  An unexpected call, email or direct message
-  A guarantee that your money can be recovered
-  A request for an upfront “retainer,” “processing fee” or “administrative charge”
-  Pressure to provide banking information, identity documents or remote access to your device
-  Claims of working with police, regulators or government agencies that you cannot independently confirm

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre's own test is one sentence, and it is the most useful sentence in this field. If someone asks you to pay money to recover money you have already lost, it is a fraud. No legitimate service is structured that way.

If you decide to hire professional help, verify them through a contact route you found independently. Not the number they gave you. Not the number on the site they sent you to. The number on the back of your bank card, or the one published by the regulator you looked up yourself.

The CAFC puts it plainly in its own guidance: if you have been a victim of fraud in the past, there is a very good chance you will be targeted again.

The first fraud takes your money. The second one takes the last of it, and it arrives disguised as help.

And before you ask, why do people still fall for these scams? Watch out for my next post: "Why Smart People Fall for Scams."

Sources:
-  Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, Top 10 Frauds in 2025 and Recovery Pitch Alert
-  Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, Recovery Scams
-  FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, public service announcement on fictitious law firms targeting scam victims

The underlying network can be incredibly difficult to attack while the systems built around it can still have vulnerabilities.

Wallets.
Custody.
Bridges.
Exchanges.
Human access.

That's one of the things I find most interesting about crypto.
The technology can remove some forms of trust.
But it doesn't remove risk.
It often just moves the risk somewhere else.
And understanding where that risk has moved is probably more important than simply asking whether crypto is “safe” or “unsafe.”

But the withdrawal button no longer worked.

The platform published a brief notice:
“Withdrawals are temporarily suspended while we review an operational incident.”
The balance and transaction history remained visible. Trading was still available. But the assets could not leave the platform.

The client’s position was simple:
“They are our crypto-assets. Return them.”

The custody structure was not.

The client’s position was recorded in an internal ledger. The assets were pooled in omnibus wallets. Key management relied on a third-party provider, and another custodian was involved.

The agreement referred to segregation but identified no specific wallets. It also allowed withdrawals to be restricted for security, legal or compliance reasons.

So the key question was not:
“When will withdrawals reopen?”
It was:
“What exactly does the client own, and which records prove it?”

A blockchain address may confirm that assets exist. It does not show which client owns which part of an omnibus wallet.

A dashboard balance shows what the platform recorded. It does not prove that the assets are segregated from the provider’s holdings or protected from its creditors.

When something goes wrong, the real questions emerge: who legally holds the assets, who controls the private keys, and whether the client owns crypto-assets or only has a contractual claim against the platform.

Can each client position be reconciled with the assets held on-chain? Are sub-custodians involved? Can the assets be lent, pledged or staked? And in insolvency, can the client recover the assets, or must they join a queue of creditors?

For EU-authorised crypto-asset service providers, MiCA requires custodians to record each client’s rights and maintain procedures for returning crypto-assets or the means of access to them.

Client assets must be legally and operationally segregated from the provider’s estate. If another custodian is used, it must be appropriately authorised, and the client must be informed.

But segregation does not necessarily mean that every client has a separate blockchain address. A withdrawal pause is not insolvency. And an internal register offers limited protection if it cannot be reconciled with the wallets.

That is why custody due diligence must happen before the assets arrive, not after the withdrawal button disappears.

Crypto custody is not simply a balance displayed on a screen.

It is a chain of legal rights, records and controls that must work when the interface does not.

posts.title: Zondacrypto's collapse is being told as a fraud story. It's also a licensing story, and the licensing part is what actually explains how this ran for years without anyone able to s
posts.author: Damani Tilton
posts.snippet:
Zondacrypto's collapse is being told as a fraud story. It's also a licensing story, and the licensing part is what actually explains how this ran for years without anyone able to stop it.

BitBay, later rebranded Zondacrypto, was founded in Poland in 2014. Poland's own regulator, the KNF, issued warnings about the exchange back in 2018. Shortly after, the company relocated its registration to Estonia and rebranded as Zondacrypto. The exchange's own blog was blunt about why at the time: Poland "doesn't want us." It moved to the jurisdiction with less scrutiny, on purpose, and said so.

The license it landed on, an Estonian VASP, was an AML/CFT authorization. Estonia's own Financial Intelligence Unit has said publicly that this type of license was never designed to assess the safekeeping, physical existence, or liquidity of client assets. It checked money laundering controls. It never checked whether the exchange actually controlled what it claimed to hold.

When MiCA introduced a real prudential license for crypto exchanges, the CASP authorization, in late 2024, Estonia chose the maximum transition period the regulation allows: 18 months. That let Zondacrypto keep operating on its old AML only license until July 1, 2026, without ever being tested against the custody and safeguarding standards MiCA was built to enforce.
 
By the time anyone looked closely, hot wallet Bitcoin reserves had fallen 99.7 percent. The license that was supposed to be watching was never built to catch that.

Zondacrypto's whole life as a company is a case study in regulatory arbitrage: the exact same business, in the exact same country, facing the exact same customer base, ends up under looser or stricter oversight depending entirely on which jurisdiction's license it happens to hold. Nothing about the underlying business changed when it registered in Estonia instead of Poland. What changed was which rulebook applied to it, and for years, that rulebook happened to be one that never tested custody or reserves at all.
 
That cuts both ways, and the other side of it is the part regulators should sit with. A license isn't just a formality a company clears to start operating; it's supposed to be the mechanism that keeps a company honest while it operates. When the license on offer doesn't include real controls, safeguarding requirements, reserve attestation, custody segregation, someone with actual authority checking the work, a company can be fully legal and still be running with none of the guardrails that make a license worth trusting in the first place. Zondacrypto wasn't breaking its license. Its license just never asked the right questions.
  
This is precisely the gap MiCA was designed to close. The whole point of replacing a patchwork of national VASP registrations with a single EU wide CASP authorization was to stop exactly this: light touch licenses being treated as a stamp of legitimacy when they were never built to test custody, reserves, or governance.

posts.title: Analyzed the Fallback level on Ethernaut, where the receive() function allowed any address with a positive contribution to become the owner by simply sending ETH directly to the co
posts.author: muhammed anshif
posts.snippet:
Analyzed the Fallback level on Ethernaut, where the receive() function allowed any address with a positive contribution to become the owner by simply sending ETH directly to the contract.

The attack flow was straightforward: send a small contribution to meet the requirement, send ETH to trigger receive() and change ownership, then call withdraw() as the new owner to drain the funds.

This is a textbook example of improper access control. The contract placed sensitive authorization logic inside receive() without additional verification.
This vulnerability pattern exists in active projects today and has led to real financial losses. The principle remains relevant: never place ownership or authorization logic in receive() or fallback() without strict controls.

Understanding how such flaws work is essential for smart contract security and blockchain forensics.

Asset Tracing & Recovery 🔎💸

Fraud recovery depends on one critical question: where did the money go?

Asset tracing helps follow stolen funds across bank accounts, crypto wallets, companies, real estate, nominees, and cross-border structures to identify assets that may be frozen, claimed, or enforced against. ⚖️

🔍 Asset tracing may be needed for:
📈 Investment platform fraud
🪙 Crypto and blockchain scams
📊 Forex, CFD, and broker fraud
💔 Pig butchering and romance investment scams
📦 Business email compromise and payment diversion
🏠 Real estate and property fraud
📉 Ponzi schemes and high-yield investment collapses
🏢 Fraudulent fund managers and unlicensed operators

⚖️ Key tracing work may include:
✔️ Bank transaction tracing
✔️ Crypto wallet and blockchain analysis
✔️ Cross-border fund tracking
✔️ Corporate registry and shareholding research
✔️ Real estate and land registry checks
✔️ Beneficial owner and nominee identification
✔️ Forensic financial analysis
✔️ Jurisdiction-specific enforcement assessment
✔️ Asset location reports for legal action

🛡️ Strong recovery planning requires:
📂 Payment records, contracts, invoices, emails, and screenshots
🏦 Bank account details, IBANs, card data, and transfer references
🪙 Wallet addresses, exchange records, and transaction hashes
🔎 Company names, directors, domains, and linked entities
⚖️ Legal strategy for freezing orders, disclosure, and enforcement

⏳ Speed matters. Fraud operators move funds quickly through layers of accounts, crypto conversions, companies, and nominees. Early tracing can preserve the asset trail before it disappears.

Asset tracing and recovery are strongest when financial analysis, blockchain tracing, corporate research, legal strategy, freezing measures, and enforcement planning are coordinated from day one.

posts.title: The line between ethical security research and financial extortion is blurring in the crypto industry.
posts.author: Blockzeit
posts.snippet:
The line between ethical security research and financial extortion is blurring in the crypto industry.

After a massive exploit targeting the Liquid Network that compromised 4,000 Bitcoin, the self-proclaimed white-hat hackers returned 85% of the stolen assets to Blockstream while keeping 598.5 BTC.

Valued at roughly $47 million, this exorbitant bounty has sparked fierce backlash in the cryptocurrency community because of its scale and the forceful tactics used.

While white-hat bounties are standard practice designed to incentivize security researchers, industry benchmarks typically cap these rewards around $10 million or roughly 5% to 10% of the recovered funds.

In this case, the group unilaterally set a 15% bug bounty and communicated largely via Bitcoin OP_RETURN messages rather than engaging in traditional direct negotiations.

Furthermore, the researchers refused to return any funds until Blockstream proved it had successfully patched the underlying vulnerability.

The unprecedented approach leaves significant collateral damage in its wake.

Retaining such a substantial amount could create a deficit in the Liquid Network reserve backing, directly threatening Liquid Bitcoin's 1:1 peg to native Bitcoin.

As discussions around potential legal action heat up, the outcome of this dispute could set a dangerous precedent for future security disclosures and the delicate relationship between protocols and independent security researchers.

posts.title: Plant the key. Walk away. Wait for the moment that matters.
posts.author: Brian C.
posts.snippet:
Plant the key. Walk away. Wait for the moment that matters.

“Deploy now, exploit later” is the quiet operator in modern cyber conflict. It is the actor who seeds code, credentials, misconfigurations, or dormant access long before anyone notices. Sometimes it is a criminal group. Sometimes it is a state unit. Sometimes it is a contractor working under direction. The identity shifts. The pattern does not.

#What: A strategy built on patience. Instead of smashing the door today, the attacker slips a key under the mat and leaves. The goal is future leverage: data theft, paralysis, extortion, or geopolitical pressure. The defining feature is delayed activation.

#Where: Inside cloud tenants, identity providers, CI/CD pipelines, firmware, unmanaged SaaS, forgotten servers, and third‑party integrations. They hide where organisations rarely audit and survive migrations, staff turnover, and vendor churn.

#Why: Because timing is power. Waiting lets the attacker strike when defenders are distracted, under pressure, or politically exposed and accumulate layered footholds that are hard to unwind.

#When: Deployment happens during routine operations: a normal patch cycle, a rushed rollout, a contractor engagement, a supply‑chain update. Exploitation comes months or years later, when logs are gone and memories have faded.

#How: Insert something small. Ensure it blends in. Leave it dormant. Monitor from afar. Activate only when conditions favour maximum impact. Defenders counter by treating every deployment as a potential future risk: strict provenance checks, continuous validation, and aggressive removal of legacy access paths.

#PQC angle: The same patience applies to cryptographic risk. Adversaries can harvest today and decrypt later once quantum arrives. Treat every long‑lived secret, every dormant integration, and every unmanaged key as a future liability. Build crypto agility now, rotate to quantum‑safe algorithms on a schedule, and remove legacy access paths before they become tomorrow’s breach.

posts.title: Liquid BTC (the Liquid Network) is accusing "white-hack hackers" of stealing $320 million of Bitcoin from the Liquid Federation wallet "via the SideSwap PAK (Peg-out Authorization
posts.author: Evan Kohlmann
posts.snippet:
Liquid BTC (the Liquid Network) is accusing "white-hack hackers" of stealing $320 million of Bitcoin from the Liquid Federation wallet "via the SideSwap PAK (Peg-out Authorization Key)."  Liquid is nonetheless insisting that the key "was not compromised" and that deposits and withdrawals of LBTC deposits have been frozen at major crypto exchanges--as well as freezing bridge notes "so no new transactions can be submitted to the network."  

According to Liquid, their sidechain has been "effectively... paused" until the issue is resolved--and they claim that they have attempted to contact the hackers on-chain with a signed message.  

It's also not entirely clear why Liquid believes the perpetrators were specifically "white-hack" hackers, or how likely it is for the money to be returned.  So-called white hacks typically target systems in order to surface critical security vulnerabilities *before* malicious actors can gain access, not to steal $320 million worth of crypto.  It's possible that, in this case, the perpetrators are seeking some kind of bug bounty before returning the stolen funds, but that would still amount to criminal extortion.

(Source links in the comments)

We've worked cases where perpetrators tried to reframe a straightforward theft as a 'security research' bounty after the fact — the tell is almost always the same: real bug bounty terms are pre-agreed, not unilaterally imposed after the funds are already moved.

posts.title: Two government departments. Two R5 million fines. Neither was for failing to have a privacy policy. 🇿🇦
posts.author: PrivIQ
posts.snippet:
Two government departments. Two R5 million fines. Neither was for failing to have a privacy policy. 🇿🇦 

South Africa's Information Regulator SA laid out its enforcement record at a media briefing on 31 August 2026 — ten years after the Regulator was established, five since POPIA's enforcement provisions came into force.

The Department of Justice and Constitutional Development was fined R5 million. Not for the 2021 ransomware attack itself, but for missing the 31-day deadline on the enforcement notice that followed — the notice ordering it to fix the lapsed antivirus and intrusion detection licences that let the attack through in the first place.

The Department of Basic Education's R5 million fine, for publishing matric results alongside learners' exam numbers, has now been taken to the Supreme Court of Appeal.

Both are still unresolved, years later. Which is exactly why the Regulator is asking Parliament for immediate fines — removing the 31-day grace period entirely. As it stands, an organisation that complies within those 31 days can't be fined at all.

If that changes, the room to fix what an enforcement notice finds disappears with it.

The pattern running through every case named: a licence renewal nobody tracked, a consent mechanism nobody revisited, a data field collected out of habit. A policy document doesn't catch those. A spreadsheet doesn't flag them in time.

PrivIQ tracks controls, owners and evidence continuously — so you'd know today if something lapsed last month, and could prove it if asked.

Could you?

#POPIA #DataPrivacy #Compliance #PrivIQ
posts.reason: South African regulator enforcement case on ransomware and compliance failures speaks directly to compliance officers and legal teams facing regulatory consequences, with actionable compliance framing.

comments.text: The detail that the DoJ fine was for missing the enforcement notice deadline, not the 2021 ransomware attack itself, is the part worth sitting with — it shows regulators increasingly punish the failure to remediate rather than the incident, which changes what 'compliance' needs to look like after a breach.

If the 31-day grace period is removed, how are organisations expected to demonstrate remediation was already underway before the notice — is documented evidence from before the finding enough, or does it need to predate the incident entirely?

We've seen the same pattern in ransomware cases elsewhere: the breach itself is rarely the sole basis for liability, it's the lapsed licence or unrevisited control that gets flagged afterward as the real failure — and that's exactly the kind of thing that only shows up if someone was tracking it continuously, not retrospectively.

posts.title: India’s next cybersecurity challenge is not buying more security tools.
posts.author: Parul Mishra
posts.snippet:
India’s next cybersecurity challenge is not buying more security tools.
It is making the entire digital enterprise resilient.
CERT-In handled 2,041,360 cybersecurity incidents during 2024—approximately 28% more than in 2023. At the same time, India’s cybersecurity product ecosystem has expanded to more than 400 companies, generating combined revenue of USD 4.46 billion in 2025.
These numbers reveal both sides of India’s cybersecurity story: rapidly expanding risk and an equally significant innovation opportunity.
As Indian enterprises accelerate cloud adoption, AI deployment, digital payments, connected infrastructure and third-party integration, the traditional security perimeter is disappearing. Cybersecurity can no longer remain restricted to the SOC or the IT department—it must become an enterprise-wide business priority.
In my view, five areas will increasingly shape the CISO agenda:
🔴 Identity as the new security perimeter
With distributed workforces, cloud applications and machine identities, controlling “who or what has access” is becoming as critical as protecting the network.
🔴 AI-powered attacks—and AI-enabled defence
AI is increasing the speed and sophistication of phishing, social engineering and vulnerability exploitation. Security teams must use AI responsibly to improve detection, investigation and response.
🔴 Cloud, API and application security
Digital transformation is expanding the attack surface. Security must be integrated into application development and cloud architecture—not applied after deployment.
🔴 Third-party and supply-chain resilience
An enterprise can have strong internal controls and still be exposed through vendors, partners, software dependencies and interconnected ecosystems.
🔴 Cyber resilience over cyber prevention
No organization can assume that every attack will be prevented. The more important question is: How quickly can the business detect, contain, recover and continue operating?
This shift also creates an important opportunity for cybersecurity companies.
The organizations that will win are not necessarily those offering the greatest number of features. They will be the ones that can translate technology into measurable business outcomes—reduced exposure, faster response, regulatory readiness, operational continuity and stronger digital trust.
India does not only need more cybersecurity products.
It needs stronger collaboration among CISOs, technology providers, policymakers, researchers and business leaders—supported by solutions that address industry-specific risks and enterprise realities.
What do you believe will dominate the Indian CISO agenda over the next 12–24 months: AI security, identity, cloud exposure, ransomware or third-party risk?
Sources: CERT-In Annual Report 2024 and DSCI Indian Cybersecurity Product Landscape Report 3.0.

Autonomous AI agents need a way to talk to each other. They need to find services, negotiate prices, and pay for tasks. By 2026, this becomes the standard way for AI to work.

Think of it as micro-services, but for agents.

Here are the core components of an A2A marketplace:

• Agent: A process that uses an API and holds cryptographic keys for payments.
• Marketplace: A layer that helps agents find each other and holds funds in escrow.
• Capability Descriptor: A schema that tells a buyer what an agent can do and how much it costs.
• Settlement Token: A stablecoin used to pay for tasks with low fees.
• Reputation: A score based on past successes or failures.

How the workflow works:

1. Register: The seller lists their service on the marketplace.
2. Discover: The buyer searches for the specific service they need.
3. Quote: The buyer checks the price and gets a signed quote.
4. Escrow and Call: The buyer sends funds to the marketplace. The marketplace calls the seller and releases the money only if the task succeeds.
5. Feedback: Both agents update their reputation scores after the task.

Building these systems requires careful handling of keys, retries, and gas fees. You must ensure the buyer gets what they pay for and the seller gets paid for their work.

posts.title: Many mid-market companies finance growth with debt while leaving one of their lowest-cost sources of working capital unused: customer deposits and milestone payments.
posts.author: Karena Bell
posts.snippet:
Many mid-market companies finance growth with debt while leaving one of their lowest-cost sources of working capital unused: customer deposits and milestone payments.

That’s not a sales issue. It’s a cash-timing decision that affects net profit, borrowing costs, and financial health clarity.

I’d start with 3 practical questions.

1. Which orders or projects can reasonably carry a deposit without weakening competitiveness or customer trust?

2. Can deposit terms be standardized by order size, delivery risk, and material commitment rather than negotiated from scratch every time?

3. Once collected, can those deposits fund materials and production inputs before the company draws on its credit line?

The discipline matters because revenue growth can consume cash long before it produces cash.

A well-designed deposit structure shortens that gap, protects margin improvement, and gives leaders more control over growth without automatically increasing debt.

The objective isn’t to push customers for cash indiscriminately.

It’s to align payment timing with the economic reality of the order, especially when the company commits capital well before delivery.

In my experience, the best deposit policies are clear, consistent, and tied to genuine cost exposure.

Would your current order terms support growth with more customer-funded working capital, or are they quietly making your balance sheet do all the work?

posts.title: ETA gets discussed as though it were a single path to business ownership. In reality, there are several distinct models, each with different economics, risk, control and investor i
posts.author: Mark Wendaur IV, Esq.
posts.snippet:
ETA gets discussed as though it were a single path to business ownership. In reality, there are several distinct models, each with different economics, risk, control and investor involvement.

That flexibility is part of what makes entrepreneurship through acquisition attractive.

Instead of building a company from zero, an entrepreneur can acquire an existing business with customers, employees, revenue and operating history already in place.

But the path to ownership can look very different depending on the model.

1. Traditional Search Fund

Investors fund the search and typically provide much of the equity for the eventual acquisition.

The searcher benefits from committed backing, experienced investors and a strong support network.

The tradeoff is dilution and governance. Searcher ownership often lands around 20–25%, with investors maintaining meaningful board and oversight rights.

2. Self-Funded Search

The entrepreneur funds the search personally, or with a small group of supporters, and raises acquisition capital after identifying a target.

This model can preserve significantly more ownership, often 50–70%, depending on the financing structure.

That creates greater upside and independence, but also more personal financial exposure and less institutional support.

3. Independent Sponsor

The entrepreneur or deal lead sources an acquisition first and then raises capital on a deal-by-deal basis.

There is generally no committed search fund upfront.

The model offers flexibility and can create attractive economics across multiple transactions, but capital is not guaranteed until a deal is found and investors are assembled.

4. Micro Private Equity or Committed Capital Vehicle 

Rather than acquiring one company and becoming its long-term CEO, a micro-PE model may involve acquiring and overseeing multiple smaller businesses.

Capital can come from a committed pool or be raised deal by deal.

The model can provide institutional credibility and the ability to build a portfolio, but it usually means less individual ownership in any one business and greater structural complexity.

The important point is that ETA is broader than “search funds.”

Different models offer different combinations of:

• ownership
• autonomy
• investor support
• personal risk
• capital availability
• governance
• ability to pursue multiple acquisitions

For someone considering business ownership, that range of options is a feature, not a complication.

The better first question may not be:

“What business should I buy?”

It may be:

“What kind of owner do I want to become?”

You build autonomous agents. Now you need to make money from them.

Traditional APIs use API keys and complex billing. This creates extra work for you. I found a better way using crypto micro-payments.

I built an agent that uses the x402 protocol on Base. This allows you to charge for every request.

How it works:

• A user calls your agent.
• They must send a tiny amount of USDC first.
• The x402 gateway checks the payment on the Base network.
• If the payment is valid, the agent runs.
• If not, the gateway returns a 402 error.

Why use Base?

Transfers on Base cost fractions of a cent. You can charge $0.01 per call without losing money to fees. You also avoid fraud and chargebacks.

The Architecture:

- x402 Gateway: A Cloudflare Worker script. It reads the payment header and verifies the USDC transfer.
- Agent Worker: A Python service. It runs a lightweight LLM like Llama-3 to decide which tools to use.
- Tool Orchestrator: A system that connects your agent to real-world data like price feeds or scrapers.
- Result Cache: A storage layer to prevent running the same expensive query twice.

The Trade-offs:

This method adds a small amount of latency because you must wait for payment confirmation. If you need sub-second responses, use off-chain billing. If you want a trustless revenue stream, use x402.

This setup keeps your agent secure. The gateway does not store private keys. It only checks the treasury address for incoming funds.

posts.author: Nirenj George
posts.snippet:
🚨 ToxicPanda 2.0: Android malware is getting smarter

A new evolution of the ToxicPanda Android banking malware demonstrates how attackers are moving beyond traditional overlay attacks.

The malware now abuses VPN permissions to control network traffic and block Google Play/Play Protect communications, potentially interfering with security checks and updates.

It also supports 167 remote commands, targets 349 banking, financial, crypto and e-wallet apps across 16 countries, and can harvest PINs and credentials through sophisticated overlays.

More concerning is its abuse of Android Accessibility Services and Wireless ADB. By enabling Developer Options and Wireless Debugging, ToxicPanda can obtain shell-level access and bypass normal permission controls.

🔐 Key takeaway for mobile banking security:
Application-layer protection alone is no longer enough. Defense-in-depth must include runtime protection, behavioral detection, device integrity, Accessibility/ADB monitoring, network controls and transaction-level fraud detection.

Mobile threats are increasingly attacking the trust boundaries between the OS, security services and banking applications.
